summary: CropShifter helps a farmer choose the next crop rotation for one field. The farmer marks the field on a map, picks a goal (keep the soil, improve it, or income) and enters the crops of the last years. The app compares the current rotation with the three best alternatives for that goal. Each one is scored on soil health and climate resilience against 45 years (1981–2025) of NASA POWER data for that exact field, with slope from NASADEM. Every card shows the evidence, the data gaps and the risks to check locally, and lists regions with a similar climate and the yields they reported. Income is a replay of past years at today's prices, not a forecast. It works for any land register parcel in Poland and for fields in Iowa (in current demo), on a phone or a laptop. The tool supports the farmer's judgment and does not replace it.
details:
Try it: https://cropshifter-demo.vercel.app/?lang=en (English; add ?lang=pl for Polish). Code: https://github.com/startupowe1konto1/NASA-Space-Apps-Hackathon. Animated pitch deck: https://cropshifter-demo.vercel.app/pitch/

WHAT IT DOES

In six steps on a phone or laptop:

1. Find the field: a Polish land register parcel (by number or by tapping the map), an address, or a drawn outline. Try parcel 302116_5.0015.28/1, a 22 ha field in Uzarzewo near Poznań.

2. Pick a goal: keep my soil, improve my soil, or income.

3. Mark the crops of the last two or three years.

4. Set priorities (water, forage, nitrogen, erosion, organic matter) and crops you will not grow.

5. Compare four rotation cards: the current rotation and the three best others for the goal.

6. "Switch or stay?": the best rotation next to the current one, with income.

Soil health and climate resilience come first on every card, whatever the goal; money enters the ranking only under the income goal. Every score has a low–high range and a confidence label. Each card has five sections (why it was suggested, evidence, benefits, data gaps, risks for local review) and a month-by-month strip that shows when the soil lies bare and which months were hit by drought, heat or frost in the field's record. Each number names its dataset, resolution, period and whether it is observed, a model estimate or our calculation. Missing data stays missing, with the reason.

HOW THE ENGINE WORKS, STEP BY STEP

1. Climate record: NASA POWER monthly and daily data for the field, 1981–2025 (rain, root-zone wetness, maximum temperature, frost days, evapotranspiration).

2. Soil from ISRIC SoilGrids (USDA SSURGO in the USA), slope from NASADEM.

3. Crop list for the country; crops that FAO GAEZ v4 rates unsuitable at the field are dropped.

4. Current rotation: the shortest repeating cycle in the farmer's crop history.

5. Candidates: one-step changes to the current rotation, then every 2- to 5-year rotation from the crop list, with and without a cover crop (up to 300). Excluded crops and impossible sowing dates are filtered out.

6. Soil health (0–100): nitrogen (legume credit minus leaching from rain in bare months), organic matter (humus balance, faster breakdown in warm and wet climates), erosion (USLE cover factor × monthly rain × slope) and pest-cycle break.

7. Climate resilience (0–100): for each crop and each of the 45 years, drought (root-zone wetness below the 20th percentile of that calendar month), heat (3+ days above the crop's threshold) and frost in the crop's sensitive months. Score = share of crop-years with no hit.

8. Income: each past year replayed at today's prices, costs and payments, with yield losses from the same hazard checks. Not a forecast.

9. Ranking by goal with published weights. Under "keep my soil" and "income", no rotation more than 5 soil points below the current one is offered.

10. Similar fields: the field's NASA POWER climate is compared with 558 regions (473 US counties, 85 European NUTS 2 regions); the closest that grow a crop of the rotation show their reported yields.

Every weight, threshold, crop trait and price is a row in the repo with the title, URL and page of the document it came from. A check rejects rows without a source.

BENEFITS

A farmer sees how a rotation would have fared on their own field through 45 years of weather, and what the data does not know. An advisor can use it at the kitchen table, with every number traceable to its source.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A first conversation tool for farmers and advisors that is honest about uncertainty and easy to extend: a new country needs a crop list and money tables, not a new engine. Next, the farmer will be able to replace any public value the engine used with their own (soil class or a lab soil test, manure, irrigation, their own yields and prices) and see the cards scored again, with each such value marked as the farmer's data.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Leaflet with Leaflet-Geoman, proj4, zod, zustand, Tailwind CSS; Vitest and Playwright tests; Vercel hosting. English and Polish interface. The pitch deck is a static Three.js page.

LIMITS

Crop lists and money tables exist for Poland and Iowa only; elsewhere the app shows the climate record. NASA POWER is a model estimate on a grid of about 50 km, not a measurement on the field. The rule tables come from published agronomy sources and need review by a local advisor. On the two demo field buttons of the hosted app, the current rotation is shown with illustrative scores below every option, labelled as such on screen; any other field shows the engine's own result.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources, NASA Langley Research Center), daily and monthly agroclimatology, 1981–2025, about 50 km grid, model estimate: drought, heat and frost years for the field, growing-season water balance, the climate resilience score, the hazard marks on the calendar and the yield losses in the income replay.
NASADEM elevation (NASA JPL), via Microsoft Planetary Computer: slope of the field, which feeds the erosion score.
NASA POWER climatology: climate features used to find regions with a similar climate.
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services): Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2, MODIS Terra corrected reflectance and Blue Marble imagery in the pitch deck.
NASA 3D Resources: Landsat 8 model in the pitch deck.
